Participation in Interactive Lecture

This page is about one specific part of a class session: the interactive lecture, where I revisit material and expect you to join in (step 5 of a typical cycle in Course Format and Materials). The in-class quizzes, exercises, notes checks, and other ways of earning engagement points work differently and are described in Grading Policies.

Think of what follows as a rubric for raising your hand.

First, Some Reassurance

I welcome participation of any kind. If you have something to say, say it. The room is better for it, and I would rather have a lively, half-formed thought than silence.

Only some kinds of participation earn engagement points, though, and those are the subject of this page. That is not a bait and switch: the room benefits from all of it, while the points measure one narrower thing.

If you are not the hand-raising type, I encourage you to push yourself anyway — it gets easier, and it is a skill worth having. But know that most historians are introverts, and that you can comfortably reach the full 100 engagement points without speaking up often. Many more points are available over the semester than you need, from quizzes, exercises, notes checks, and office hours. So treat this as an opportunity rather than a source of stress.

What Earns Points

Two things, together:

  1. It demonstrates engagement with the assigned course materials, and
  2. It helps other students deepen their understanding of them.

The Gold Standard: Work from the Assigned Readings

The most reliable way to earn points is to reference the assigned readings directly, and the primary sources above all.

Here is an invented example. Suppose a letter home from a soldier at the front is among the assigned sources, and I have just argued in lecture that war and revolution were one continuous process rather than two separate events.

Reinforcing the point: “On page 34, the soldier says the men in his unit had stopped telling the officers apart from the grain speculators. That seems to support what you just said about continuity — he is already describing a political enemy while he is still in uniform.”

Complicating it: “That letter is dated eight months before February, though. If he already saw it that way, does that complicate the idea of a continuous process, or does it mean the continuity began earlier than the war?”

Either move works. Reinforcing is not flattery and complicating is not impertinence — both show you read the thing and thought about how it sits against the argument.

Read the passage out loud, and give the page number. This is not a formality. It lets everyone else find the full context, follow your reasoning, and add the passage to their own notes (see Note-Taking). A contribution that does this is doing work for the whole room, which is half the criteria above.

Questions Count, If They Do the Same Work

A question can earn points as readily as a claim. The test is the same.

“What does this mean?” will always be answered and is always welcome, but it does not on its own show engagement with the material, so it does not earn points. Compare:

“On page 12 the chronicler treats the city’s surrender as a foregone conclusion — he gives the siege barely a sentence. But the tax register from last week suggests the city was still collecting revenue two years later. How should I square those?”

That question notices something real in one source, holds it against a second, and hands the room a problem worth having. Noticing where your sources disagree is harder than restating what one of them says, and it is worth more.

Building on Each Other

Responding to a classmate counts, and often counts for more than addressing me:

  • answering another student’s question;
  • extending a point someone else made, with evidence;
  • disagreeing with a classmate, as long as you disagree with the argument and say what in the material leads you elsewhere.

A discussion is something a class does together. The best sessions are the ones where students talk to each other and I mostly moderate.

Material from Outside the Course

I am genuinely interested in connections you draw to things beyond the syllabus: another course, your own reading, research you have done. The one condition is that it be grounded and sourced.

I say “specific” because I may well ask you to back it up — to tell us how you know what you think you know. That question is not a trap and it is not a reprimand. It is the ordinary move of the discipline, the same one I would expect from a colleague, and asking it of you is a sign that I find the claim interesting enough to pursue.

“I’m not certain — I think it was in a book about the Mongol postal system, and I can find the title” is a perfectly good answer. Vagueness is fine. Inventing a source is not.

What Doesn’t Earn Points

Not an exhaustive list, but the common cases:

  • “What does this mean?” on its own, or any question the reading or the syllabus already answers.
  • An opinion with nothing under it: “I thought the author was biased,” with no passage and no reason.
  • Restating, in different words, something I or another student just said.
  • A page number with nothing attached to it. The citation is not what earns the point; what you do with it is.
  • Talking frequently. Volume is not the measure. Four genuinely illuminating contributions across a semester will do more for you than forty fillers.

On the Subjectivity of All This

Judging participation is a subjective business, but it is not an arbitrary one. The two criteria at the top of this page are the whole basis for it, and everything above is an attempt to show you what they look like in practice.

I do not award a fixed number of points per session. A single contribution that genuinely opens up a source can be worth more than several routine ones, and I would rather keep the room’s judgment flexible than hand out credit by the clock.

Points are recorded as they happen, and like evaluation grades they are not reopened afterwards (see Grading Policies). If you want to talk about how to participate more effectively, that is a conversation I am always glad to have in office hours — and one that earns engagement points in its own right.
